overview: This file contains two distinct State Department records concerning economic development and American commercial interests in Japanese-controlled Manchuria. The principal despatch, sent from Dairen in June 1935, reports the arrival of 775 American Merino sheep for a crossbreeding program intended to raise Manchuria’s wool yield substantially. An apparently unrelated Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum from November 1934 summarizes a diplomatic question about whether an American company’s crude-oil sales proposal should be forwarded to the Manchuria Oil Company through the consular service.

subfiles.title: Despatch on importing American sheep to increase Manchurian wool production
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: Reports the arrival at Dairen of American Merino sheep intended for crossbreeding and improvement of Manchuria’s wool yield.
subfiles.summary: Grummon reports that 775 Merino sheep from Utah, Wyoming, and Nevada were unloaded at Dairen following experiments by the South Manchuria Railway Agricultural Experimental Station at Kungchuling and a visit to the United States by two officials of the Manchukuo Mongolian Affairs Department. The flock included 723 rams, with 550 animals consigned to Manchukuo’s Department of Industry. Native sheep reportedly yielded about 2.5 pounds of relatively poor wool per head, whereas experimental crossbred sheep produced 7–10 pounds; officials therefore hoped to increase annual Manchurian production from approximately nine million to 28–40 million pounds.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on proposed crude-oil sale to the Manchuria Oil Company
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Tokyo Embassy despatch concerning whether an American crude-oil sales letter should be delivered to the Manchuria Oil Company through the consular service.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum summarizes Tokyo despatch No. 1014 of October 18, 1934, concerning a sales proposal from the Export Petroleum Company of California, Ltd., to the Manchuria Oil Company. The American Consul at Dairen withheld the letter because of the unusual oil-trade situation in Manchuria, and Ambassador Grew endorsed that judgment during a visit to Dairen. Because the Department had supplied no guidance on the desirability of such sales, the Embassy could not decide whether to forward the proposal; the Consul apparently favored returning it to the sender with an explanation.

interest: The sheep despatch provides unusually precise evidence about a state-backed livestock-improvement project, including the animals’ American states of origin, allocation among Manchukuo agencies, and projected effects on wool output. It is useful for studying agricultural modernization, American exports, and economic planning under Japanese-sponsored Manchukuo. The juxtaposition of the unrelated oil memorandum—carrying a different decimal-file number—also illustrates the imperfect filing, cross-referencing, or later bundling of State Department records and preserves evidence of diplomatic caution toward commerce with Manchurian monopoly enterprises.
